project.topic: What if 8.3 billion people on Earth drank the ocean at the same time?
project.title: What if 8.3 billion people drank the ocean at the same time?
project.audience: Curious international viewers who enjoy surprising Earth-scale comparisons and playful counterfactual science.
project.core_question: Could all 8.3 billion people make a visible dent in the ocean by drinking together?
project.viewer_takeaway: One liter each totals 8.3 billion liters yet only about 23 nanometers of equivalent global mean sea-level change; emptying the ocean would require about 161 billion liters per person.

captions.highlights_policy: The physical consequence of each scene in accent colour; at most two emphasis phrases per scene.

audio.voice_style: Crisp, urgent, fascinated adult male; high-tension simulation narrator; brisk opening cadence
audio.music_direction: Playful escalating plucks and warm ocean pulse, dropping for 0.3 seconds before the 23nm reversal; dry final finish.
audio.sfx_direction: Restrained intake bubbles, straw handling, pool water and volume-case accents. No destruction, giant suction or invented tsunami.

scientific_model.baseline_reality: The oceans, seas and bays contain approximately 1.338e21 liters of water. Ocean surface area is approximately 361.934e12 square meters. Normal seawater is salty and does not safely hydrate humans.
scientific_model.counterfactual_change: Exactly the user-specified 8.3 billion people begin taking seawater together. Start with an explicitly hypothetical one-liter-per-person withdrawal, then calculate larger mathematical quotas.
assumptions: 8.3 billion is the stipulated participant count, not a claim about a live population census.

Every participant is granted access to seawater without entering the water or displacing it. Representative people stand on a grounded pier and use hoses; logistics are outside this arithmetic thought experiment.
One liter per person is the chosen first benchmark, not the capacity of one normal gulp or a recommended quantity. Withdrawing and drinking are represented as one stylized intake event.
Withdrawn water is kept out of the sea during the calculation; return flows, tides, rain, basin elasticity and gravity fingerprints are neglected.
Volume divided by fixed surface area gives an equivalent eventual global mean change, not an instantaneous uniform local shoreline response. Tiny changes are never visibly exaggerated.
Reference swimming pools have explicit interior dimensions 50 by 25 by 2 meters: 2.5 million liters each. No current Olympic standard is asserted.

The one-millimeter and whole-ocean personal shares are mathematical scaling cases, not quantities actually consumed. Grounded tanks display equivalent capacity; the huge tank is a volume comparison, not an engineering proposal.
No dose-specific medical outcome, immediate deaths or global catastrophe is predicted.
causal_chain: 8.3 billion participants times one liter each removes 8.3 billion liters.
That equals 3,320 reference pools, producing a misleadingly huge-looking volume.
Spread over the ocean surface, the same volume is only 22.93 nanometers of equivalent global mean drop, invisible beside ordinary waves.
A one-millimeter equivalent drop instead requires about 43,606 liters per person.
The full ocean divided among participants is about 161.2 billion liters each, far beyond human drinking capacity.
Seawater additionally causes net water loss; a finite person withdraws their straw while the coast remains visually unchanged.
uncertainties: Ocean volume and area are approximate estimates; derived HUD values are appropriately rounded.
The surface-area approximation is appropriate for the tiny benchmark and one millimeter, not a complete ocean-drainage sea-level model. The full-drain result divides volume only.
Shader waves and finite straw acting illustrate intake; there is no fluid solver, biological dose model or actual 8.3-billion-character render.

claims.statement: One liter each for 8.3 billion people totals 8.3 billion liters, or 3,320 reference pools.
claims.reasoning: 8.3e9 times 1 L; 50*25*2 m3 times 1000 L/m3 is 2.5e6 L per pool.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Keep everyone-combined scope clear; do not present one liter as one ordinary gulp.

claims.statement: The one-liter benchmark corresponds to about 23 nanometers of equivalent global mean sea-level drop.
claims.reasoning: 8.3e9 L /1000 /361.934e12 m2 =2.2932358e-8 m. NASA provides the area/conversion method.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Say average level and show unchanged natural waves, not retreating shore or an enlarged physical drop.

claims.statement: Draining the full ocean would require about 161 billion liters per person.
claims.reasoning: USGS volume 1.338e9 km3 *1e12 L/km3 divided by 8.3e9 participants =1.612048e11 L each.
claims.presentation_guardrail: A mathematical personal quota, not a physiologically possible drink or actual construction.

claims.statement: A one-millimeter equivalent global mean drop costs about 43,600 liters per person.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Explicitly transition to scaling the math; never depict a human actually consuming this tank.

claims.statement: Real seawater contains about 3.5% salts by mass and can cause net water loss rather than hydration.
claims.reasoning: NOAA gives normal salinity around35 parts per thousand and explains loss of more water in urine to excrete the excess salt.
claims.presentation_guardrail: No instantaneous dehydration animation or specific dose/death forecast.

sources.name: USGS: ocean, sea and bay water volume
NASA JPL VESL: ocean area and global mean volume/area conversion
NOAA: normal seawater salinity about 35 parts per thousand

creative_direction.logline: A synchronized ocean-drinking challenge escalates from one liter to thousands of pools, then reverses at an invisible 23-nanometer drop and impossible personal quotas.
creative_direction.visual_identity: Premium bright coastal miniatures and real scale volume comparisons; reference-inspired boxless white top-left numbers over textured 3D subjects.
creative_direction.lighting: Coastal late-morning directional sun, soft blue sky fill and controlled water reflections. The same palette anchors pier, pool complex and grounded volume tanks.
creative_direction.camera_language: Eye-level straw/hand setup, active front-facing crowd, real pool-to-aerial reveal, calm shoreline contact, and human-to-tank scale reveals. Numeric camera keys own all moves.
creative_direction.motion_language: Finite attention, supported straw grip and withdrawal; simultaneous intake; pool filling as an explicit capacity comparison; tank fill and settled capacity views; ordinary waves never become a fake tsunami.
creative_direction.world_scale_policy: Metres. 50x25x2m pool cavities and capacity-derived tank dimensions. Magnification belongs in the camera; never enlarge a 23nm sea-level drop.
creative_direction.opening_hook: You slurp the ocean while everyone joins; a physical straw and active representative crowd make the action immediate.
creative_direction.mid_video_rehook: Thousands of poolfuls make only a 23-nanometer average ocean-level change. The beach does not visibly move.
creative_direction.ending_payoff: Human bodies and salty water are the bottleneck; the original straw lowers while the ocean remains visually unchanged.
creative_direction.loop_connection: Return to the same straw, pier and normal waves after impossible mathematical quotas; no narrated rewind.
creative_direction.asset_policy: Reuse registered ocean/sky, boat, bottle, humanoid, grounded-motion, modeling, editorial HUD and audio/render kits. Add reusable physically dimensioned pool and capacity-tank components after registry search found none.

distribution.seo_integrity_note: Use oceanography, scale and physiology qualifiers; no false global-disaster or population-statistic claims.
